ARCHIVE: This is the pattern people need to see. One side offers a concession. The other side answers with force. On March 7 2003 Arafat signaled he was reducing his own political power. He nominated Mahmoud Abbas to be prime minister of the Palestinian Authority. Serious movement on the Road Map finally began. That was the compromise path. In the same period Israel tried but failed to kill Abdel Aziz Rantisi, a key Hamas leader. It was the first of seven targeted assassinations in five days. So one side moved toward compromise. The other side kept killing. Israel either does not know it or does not care. When people watch their leaders and relatives get killed, grief turns into moral outrage. Martyrdom gives resistance deep emotional purpose. Constant threat activates survival instincts and group solidarity. And compromise starts to feel like betraying the dead. So fear and force do the opposite of what Israel claims. They pass trauma from one generation to the next. They deepen hatred on both sides. They do not produce obedience. Israel has been killing Palestinian leaders for decades. Today there is still no Palestinian submission and no surrender. There will not be. Because killing a leader does not weaken the will of the people. It builds it. Every funeral becomes a reason to keep going. You cannot bomb a people into giving up their land. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Palestine # Israel # Zionist # HumanRights # MiddleEast

ARCHIVE: Late March 2002 a Hamas suicide bomber killed thirty Israelis at a Passover seder. The Palestinian Authority denounced the attack and pledged to prosecute. Sharon launched Operation Defensive Shield. Israeli forces retook virtually all major Palestinian areas in the West Bank. Bush knew this would wreck America image in the Arab world and hurt the war on terror. On April 4 he demanded Sharon "halt the incursions and begin withdrawal." Two days later: "withdrawal without delay." On April 7 Condoleezza Rice told reporters "without delay means without delay. It means now." Powell flew to the region. The lobby went after Powell first. Neocons in the vice president office and the Pentagon pushed Bush and Rice to drop the pressure. Kagan and Kristol wrote in the Weekly Standard that Powell had "virtually obliterated the distinction between terrorists and those fighting terrorists." David Brooks called the trip "a disaster as opposed to an unmitigated disaster." Netanyahu said before Powell even landed that the trip "won't amount to anything." Powell deputy called him from Washington: "I am holding back the fucking gates here. They are eating cheese on you." Powell later called it "ten of the most miserable days imaginable." Then they went after Bush. DeLay and Trent Lott visited the White House on April 10 and warned him to back off. Falwell and Gary Bauer sent a letter demanding the administration "end pressure" on Sharon. The White House was flooded with calls. The next day Bush aides phoned Falwell to reassure him Bush stood behind Sharon. On April 11, one week after demanding withdrawal, Ari Fleischer said Bush believed Sharon was "a man of peace." Troops had not withdrawn. Bush repeated it on April 18 and claimed Sharon had responded satisfactorily. He had not. Congress finished the job. May 2: Senate 94 to 2, House 352 to 21, both calling the two countries "engaged in a common struggle against terrorism" and condemning "the ongoing support of terror by Yasir Arafat." May 9: a House subcommittee added $200 million for Israel against White House opposition. Powell tried to stop it. Powell lost. Bush signed. Chemi Shalev of Ma'ariv reported what Sharon aides were saying privately: "Sharon saw the white in President Bush eyes, they bragged, and the President blinked first." Spain leading daily El Pais summed it up: "If a country weight is measured by its degree of influence on events, the superpower is not the USA but Israel." this is the whole machine in one week. The president of the United States gave a direct order to a foreign leader. The Israeli lobby called in Congress, the evangelicals, the neocon press, and the money. Seven days later the president called the man who defied him "a man of peace." That is not a debate. That is a leash. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Palestine # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: In 2002 and 2003 the Bush administration pushed the Road Map. It was a Quartet plan, US, EU, UN, and Russia, meant to lead to a negotiated Palestinian state by 2005. Sharon had no interest in it. The Washington Post editorial in December 2002 said it plainly. Sharon told voters he supported the plan. But his envoys were "harshly criticizing the draft road map" in meetings with US officials. And Sharon himself dismissed the plan as "irrelevant" in a cabinet meeting. Chemi Shalev wrote in the Forward that Sharon "strategic goal" was "to undermine the road map." Conference of Presidents chairman Mortimer Zuckerman called it the "road map to nowhere." When Bush said in March 2003 he was pushing the plan, National Security Adviser Condoleezza Rice met Jewish leaders at the White House. The aim, according to Ha'aretz, was "to neutralize American Jewish reservations about the plan." She failed. ADL head Abraham Foxman and Conference of Presidents vice chairman Malcolm Hoenlein were especially critical. AIPAC sponsored a letter to Bush urging him not to pressure Israel on the Road Map. By early May 85 senators and 283 representatives had signed it. Krauthammer wrote in the Washington Post that proceeding along the Road Map with Arafat in power was "diplomatic suicide." But the real story came out later. The Financial Times reported that Elliott Abrams and Stephen Hadley, two key players on the National Security Council, secretly assured Sharon "that he would not face US pressure over the road map." So while Bush was publicly pushing the plan, his own staff was privately telling Sharon he could ignore it. In June 2003 Bush made one mild criticism of Israel over helicopter attacks. Just one. The lobby mobilized. DeLay met Bush aides and threatened a congressional resolution supporting Israel if Bush kept criticizing. On June 11 Bush hosted a dinner at the White House with one hundred Jewish leaders. Hoenlein, who met Bush privately that evening, said the president "and others at the White House recognized that their reaction could be counterproductive." By June 12 the White House did a U-turn. Fleischer said "The issue is not Israel" it is "terrorists who are killing in an attempt to stop a hopeful process." Later that month the House passed a resolution 399 to 5 expressing "solidarity with the Israeli people" and saying Israel was fully justified in using force against terrorism. My analysis is this is the double game in one story. Bush announces a peace plan in public. His own NSC staff secretly tells Sharon not to worry about it. Sharon says yes in public and kills it in private. The lobby runs the Congress letter and the pressure campaign. Then one mild criticism from Bush gets crushed in 48 hours. The Road Map was dead before it was printed. And the people who killed it still got to say they support peace. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Palestine # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: July 2003 Bush said the Israeli security fence was a problem. "It is very difficult to develop confidence between the Palestinians and Israel with a wall snaking through the West Bank." Four days later Sharon stood next to Bush at the White House and said he would keep building it. Bush did not challenge him. He accepted Sharon framing that Palestinian terrorism was "the fundamental obstacle to peace." Secretary of State Colin Powell suggested the fence was an Israeli attempt to take Palestinian land. Condoleezza Rice hinted the US might deduct the fence cost from $9 billion in loan guarantees. Senator Charles Schumer made the threat openly. If the president "flouts the will of Congress and tries to penalize Israel for defending itself, Congress will do everything in its power to ensure that these loan guarantees are not held up." A senior Israeli official was not worried. "We are not under any pressure," he said. "The United States is a very vibrant democracy, and this is a very politically oriented administration. Reality is made sometimes by political constraints." In late November 2003 the US cut $289.5 million from the $3 billion in loan guarantees. It sounds big. It was not. The former director general of Israel Finance Ministry estimated it would cost Israel about $4 million a year in higher interest. That is it. No direct aid was cut. The authors call it "a weak slap on the wrist." Then in November 2003 Sharon invited Elliott Abrams, the NSC official for Near East affairs, to a secret meeting in Rome. Sharon told him he would not negotiate a settlement. He would impose his own terms on the Palestinians instead. Dov Weisglass, Sharon closest adviser, later explained the plan in plain words. "The significance of what we did is the freezing of the political process. And when you freeze that process you prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state and you prevent a discussion about the refugees, the borders and Jerusalem." He added: "The plan is actually formaldehyde. It supplies the amount of formaldehyde that is necessary so that there will not be a political process with the Palestinians." In spring 2004 Bush publicly embraced the plan. He called it a "bold courageous step" and said the world owed Sharon a "thank you." On April 14 2004 Bush reversed the stated policy of every president since Lyndon Johnson. He said Israel would not have to return virtually all the territories it occupied in 1967, and Palestinian refugees would not return to their former homes. Thomas Friedman of the New York Times summed it up in early 2004. "Mr. Sharon has the Palestinian leader Yasir Arafat under house arrest in his office in Ramallah, and he has had George Bush under house arrest in the Oval Office." My analysis is the quote from Weisglass is the most honest thing in the whole book. The plan was never about peace. It was formaldehyde. Formaldehyde preserves a dead body. That is exactly what it did to the peace process. And Bush gave the man a thank you and reversed 37 years of US policy for him. The $289 million "punishment" cost Israel $4 million a year. That is not a punishment. That is a parking ticket. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Palestine # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: While the US was pushing the Road Map and talking about a Palestinian state, Israel kept killing Palestinian leaders. Sometimes with American weapons. Sometimes at the worst possible moment for Washington. July 22 2002: Israeli forces killed Sheik Salah Shehada, a prominent Hamas leader. Fourteen others died too, including nine children. The attack scuttled a proposed Palestinian cease-fire. The White House called it "heavy handed." That was it. No consequences. The targeted assassination policy continued. March 22 2004: Israel assassinated Hamas leader Sheik Ahmed Yassin with American-made Hellfire missiles. This was seen as a serious blow to America position in the Middle East. Not just because US weapons were used. But because many in the Arab world believed the Bush administration had given Israel the green light to kill a paraplegic in a wheelchair. Jim Hoagland of the Washington Post wrote after Yassin was killed: "With the possible exception of Charles de Gaulle, no friendly foreign leader has complicated modern American diplomacy and strategy more consistently or gravely than Ariel Sharon. He pursues Israel interests with a warrior tenacity and directness that take away the breath, and the options, of everyone else." Less than a month later, on April 17 2004, Israeli forces finally killed Rantisi. My analysis is this is the trap they built for the Palestinians. Kill the leaders. Scuttle the cease-fires. Then when no moderate partner appears, say Palestinians only understand violence. You cannot negotiate with a man you are trying to kill. You cannot build a moderate Palestinian leadership while you are assassinating everyone who might lead it. The kill list was the policy. The peace process was the cover story. And they used American missiles to do it. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Palestine # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: Arafat died in November 2004. In January 2005 Mahmoud Abbas won a peaceful election that outside observers called free and fair. This was the best chance for peace in years. Abbas recognized Israel. He renounced terrorism. He wanted a negotiated settlement. And Bush had just won reelection, so he was in the strongest political position of his presidency to help him. Bush did almost nothing. Why? Because he had already committed to Sharon unilateral disengagement plan. That plan held no promise of a viable Palestinian state. The authors say Bush backing it doomed the Road Map from the start. Sharon refused to negotiate. He made it impossible for Abbas to deliver anything to the Palestinian people. Ha'aretz columnist Bradley Burston wrote just before the January 2006 Palestinian election: "If it appears to you that Israel is Hamas campaign manager in next week elections for the Palestinian parliament, few would argue, especially in Hamas." Hamas won. Now Israel had another reason not to negotiate. And the Bush administration was even less likely to push them to talk. Then the Gaza pullout collapsed. Israel pulled out in August 2005 and then cordoned off Gaza. Palestinians could not lead a decent life. Rockets continued. A soldier was captured on June 25 2006. Three days later Israel reentered Gaza. Olmert, who took over from the incapacitated Sharon, admitted it in January 2007. He told the Chinese news agency Xinhua that he had been confident unilateral withdrawal could solve the problem. He was wrong. Now, he said, "under the existing circumstances, it would be more practical to achieve a two-state solution through negotiations rather than unilateral withdrawal." A moderate Palestinian leader gets elected. He recognizes Israel and renounces violence. Israel refuses to negotiate with him because Israel does not want a viable Palestinian state. The moderate leader loses credibility because he has nothing to show for his moderation. Hamas wins the next election. Then Israel says it cannot negotiate because Hamas is in power. They created the excuse they use. Every time a moderate appears, they kill the moderate path and then blame the Palestinians for the result. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Palestine # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: In March 2007 the Arab League reissued its peace plan. The offer was big. Peace and normal relations with all twenty-two Arab states in return for Israel withdrawing from the Occupied Territories and the Golan Heights, a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital, and a negotiated solution to the refugee issue. The Saudis made clear it was a starting point, not a take-it-or-leave-it deal. Olmert was not interested. He rejected any Israeli responsibility for the refugee issue. "I will not agree to any kind of Israeli responsibility for this problem. Full stop." He said the return of even one refugee to Israel was "out of the question." Ha'aretz editorial: "A realistic government would have rushed to embrace this willingness for recognition and reconciliation." Condoleezza Rice tried anyway. She traveled to Jerusalem seven times in eight months. In early February 2007 she met fifteen major Jewish leaders and told them she would not pressure Israel and would not offer US suggestions on what a final deal might look like. The authors say this "greatly limited the secretary's effectiveness." On February 19 she brought Olmert and Abbas together. Both refused to appear with her at the press conference. The New York Times ran an editorial titled "Charade in Jerusalem." In late March she returned and raised the idea of serving as a mediator. Olmert flatly rejected it. She had to cancel the press conference. The Daily Telegraph headline: "Israel Snubs Condoleezza Rice." Behind the scenes Elliott Abrams was working against her. He was the NSC official for the Middle East. He had help from two neoconservatives in the vice president office, John Hannah and David Wurmser. Journalist Jim Lobe reported that sources said Abrams was "working systematically to undermine any prospect for serious negotiations." Daniel Levy, a former adviser in the Israeli prime minister office, described the routine. When Rice got too active, Olmert aides Yoram Turbowitz and Shalom Turgeman were dispatched to Abrams, who would "enlist Cheney to keep the president in tow." Henry Siegman of the Council on Foreign Relations said every time the US looked ready to engage seriously, Abrams met secretly with Olmert envoys in Europe to reassure them. Just before Rice arrived in February, Olmert let the media know he had spoken to Bush the day before and that "the prime minister and president see eye-to-eye." Ha'aretz reporters Aluf Benn and Shmuel Rosner wrote: "The message was unmistakable: What Rice had to say barely mattered." Philip Zelikow was Rice closest adviser at State. He gave a speech in September 2006 linking the Palestinian issue to building an anti-Iran coalition. Pro-Israel groups attacked immediately. State distanced itself the same day. Rice assured Israeli foreign minister Tzipi Livni the two issues were separate. Zelikow left the next month. He was replaced by Eliot Cohen, a neoconservative. Congress also blocked her. Bush approved $86 million to strengthen Abbas security forces. Congresswoman Nita Lowey held it up. Anthony Weiner wrote to Rice asking her to withdraw it. ZOA head Morton Klein said Bush "should be as tough on Abbas as he is on Hamas and al Qaeda." The amount was cut to $59 million with restrictions. June 2007: Hamas preempted the whole thing and seized Gaza. My analysis is this is how you sabotage a peace process without ever saying no. You do not reject the talks publicly. You send your guys to reassure the other side that nothing will happen. You block the money for the moderate. You get the president to say he sees eye-to-eye with the prime minister. And then you let the whole thing collapse and blame the side with less power. Rice traveled seven times. Seven trips. And Olmert would not even stand next to her at a press conference. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Palestine # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: The usual defense of US policy is that the president is just following the people. The polls say otherwise. April 2002. Bush had just demanded that Sharon withdraw from the West Bank. A Time/CNN poll taken April 10 and 11 found that 60 percent of Americans felt US aid to Israel should be cut off or reduced if Sharon refused to withdraw. 75 percent thought Powell should meet Arafat on his trip. Only 35 percent found Sharon trustworthy. 35 percent called him a warmonger. 20 percent called him a terrorist. 25 percent considered him an enemy of the United States. May 2003. A University of Maryland poll found over 60 percent of Americans would be willing to withhold aid to Israel if it resisted US pressure to settle the conflict. Among politically active Americans that number rose to 70 percent. 73 percent said the US should not favor either side. Only 17 percent agreed with the Bush and Sharon claim that the conflict is part of the war on terrorism. 54 percent saw it as a conflict between two national groups fighting over the same land. 55 percent had a positive view of the Road Map. When told its key elements, support rose to 74 percent. Even the ADL own 2005 survey found that 78 percent of Americans believe their government should favor neither Israel nor the Palestinians. So the public was not the obstacle. The public wanted evenhandedness. The obstacle was the Israeli lobby. Brent Scowcroft was national security adviser to the first President Bush. In October 2004 he said Sharon had George W. Bush "wrapped around his little finger." The authors put it plainly. "Absent the lobby, the Bush administration almost certainly would have been much more self-interested and hard-nosed in pushing for peace between Israel and the Palestinians." The US has done this to other states many times. It pressured Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Belarus to give up nuclear weapons. It pressured Libya to give up its weapons programs. It fought an air war over Kosovo. Putting pressure on Israel would not have been unusual. It just never happened. My analysis is this is the anti-democracy part nobody talks about. Most Americans wanted the US to pressure Israel. 60 to 78 percent depending on the poll. The Israeli lobby is a minority position. And it won every single time. So when they say America supports Israel because Americans support Israel, that is a lie. Americans wanted evenhandedness. The lobby made sure they never got it. That is not democracy. That is a foreign policy run against the voters. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Palestine # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights

ARCHIVE: Why did the United States invade Iraq? The official reasons were WMD and links to al Qaeda. Both were false. But people inside the government said the real reason out loud, and they said it before the war started. Philip Zelikow was on the president Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board, executive director of the 9/11 Commission, and later counselor to Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice. On September 10 2002 he told a University of Virginia audience that Saddam was not a direct threat to the United States. "The real threat," he said, "is the threat against Israel." Then he added: "And this is the threat that dare not speak its name, because the Europeans dont care deeply about that threat... And the American government doesnt want to lean too hard on it rhetorically, because it is not a popular sell." General Wesley Clark, the retired NATO commander, said in August 2002: "Those who favor this attack now will tell you candidly, and privately, that it is probably true that Saddam Hussein is no threat to the United States. But they are afraid that at some point he might decide if he had a nuclear weapon to use it against Israel." Ruth Wedgwood was a neoconservative academic on the Defense Policy Board. A German journalist asked her why he should support the war. "I could be impolite," she said, "and remind Germany of its special relationship with Israel. Saddam presents an existential threat to Israel. That is simply true." She did not say Iraq threatened Germany or America. Joe Klein wrote in Time magazine before the invasion: "A stronger Israel is very much embedded in the rationale for war with Iraq. It is a part of the argument that dare not speak its name, a fantasy quietly cherished by the neo-conservative faction in the Bush Administration and by many leaders of the American Jewish community." Senator Ernest Hollings said in May 2004 that the answer, which "everyone knows," is "because we want to secure our friend Israel." The ADL called his comments "reminiscent of age-old, anti-Semitic canards about a Jewish conspiracy to control and manipulate government." Hollings had long been a staunch supporter of Israel. He demanded his critics "apologize to me for talking about anti-Semitism." Michael Kinsley wrote in fall 2002 that "the lack of public discussion about the role of Israel... is the proverbial elephant in the room: Everybody sees it, no one mentions it." The reason for the silence, he said, was fear of being called an antisemite. Nathan Guttman reported in Ha'aretz two weeks before the war: "The voices linking Israel to the war are getting louder and louder... And the voices come from all directions." Bill Keller, now executive editor of the New York Times, wrote: "The idea that this war is about Israel is persistent and more widely held than you may think." In May 2005 Barry Jacobs of the American Jewish Committee acknowledged that the belief that Israel and the neoconservatives got the US to invade Iraq was "pervasive" in the US intelligence community. My analysis is the most damning thing here is that they said it themselves. Not critics. Not bloggers. The 9/11 Commission director. A retired NATO general. A member of the Defense Policy Board. A US senator. They all said the war was for Israel. And the moment anyone said it in public, the answer was not a debate. It was "you are an antisemite." That is how you keep an elephant in the room. You make everyone afraid to say it is there. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Israel did not start the campaign for the Iraq war. The neoconservatives did. But once Israel saw that Bush was serious, Israeli leaders joined in and pushed hard. And when a diplomatic path opened through UN inspections, they worked to close it. April 2002: Benjamin Netanyahu came to Washington. He met US senators and the editors of the Washington Post. He warned them that Saddam was developing nuclear weapons that could be delivered against the American homeland in suitcases or satchels. A few weeks later Ra'anan Gissen, Sharon spokesman, told a Cleveland reporter: "If Saddam Hussein is not stopped now, five years from now, six years from now, we will have to deal with an Iraq that is armed with nuclear weapons, with an Iraq that has delivery systems for weapons of mass destruction." Mid-May: Shimon Peres appeared on CNN. "Saddam Hussein is as dangerous as bin Laden," he said. The United States "cannot sit and wait" while he builds a nuclear arsenal. June: Ehud Barak wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post. He recommended the Bush administration "should, first of all, focus on Iraq and the removal of Saddam Hussein. Once he is gone there will be a different Arab world." August 12: Sharon told the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee that Iraq "is the greatest danger facing Israel." August 16, ten days before Cheney kicked off the war campaign with his VFW speech: Ha'aretz, the Washington Post, CNN, and CBS all reported that Israel was urging the US not to delay the attack. Sharon told the Bush administration that postponing "will not create a more convenient environment for action in the future." Peres told CNN "the problem today is not if, but when." Deputy Defense Minister Weizman Shiry said: "If the Americans do not do this now, it will be harder to do it in the future." CBS headline: "Israel to US: Don't Delay Iraq Attack." Peres and Sharon made sure to say they did not want to be seen as pushing America. But their public comments show the opposite. Then the inspections path opened. September 2002: Bush decided to seek UN Security Council authorization for war. Israelis were distressed. Then Saddam agreed to let UN inspectors back in. They were more worried still. Peres told reporters: "The campaign against Saddam Hussein is a must. Inspections and inspectors are good for decent people, but dishonest people can overcome easily inspections and inspectors." Sharon flew to Moscow in late September. He told Vladimir Putin, who was leading the charge for new inspections, that it was too late for them to be effective. Peres got so frustrated with the UN process that in mid-February 2003 he lashed out at France and questioned its status as a permanent member of the Security Council. Marc Perelman wrote in the Forward in mid-September 2002: "Saddam Hussein surprise acceptance of unconditional United Nations weapons inspections put Israel on the hot seat this week, forcing it into the open as the only nation actively supporting the Bush administration goal of Iraqi regime change." Israeli figures compared Saddam to Hitler and called opponents of the war appeasers. Shlomo Avineri wrote in the Los Angeles Times: "all who condemn the 1930s appeasement of Germany should reflect long and hard on whether a failure to act today against Iraq will one day be viewed the same way." The Jerusalem Post editorialized that "ousting Saddam is the linchpin of the war on terrorism, without which it is impossible to begin in earnest, let alone win." My analysis is look at the sequence. When there was no diplomatic path, Israel pushed for war. When the UN inspections path opened, Israel said inspections are useless. When France tried to keep that path alive, Peres attacked France. They did not want inspections. They did not want a deal. They wanted the war. And when it happened, they said they never pushed for it. The public record says otherwise. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Israel was not just pushing for war. It was feeding Washington intelligence about Iraq WMD that later turned out to be false. Around August 2002 news stories reported that "Israeli intelligence officials have gathered evidence that Iraq is speeding up efforts to produce biological and chemical weapons." Peres told CNN that "we think and know that he [Saddam] is on his way to acquiring a nuclear option." Ha'aretz reported that Saddam had given an "order... to Iraq's Atomic Energy Commission last week to speed up its work." Israel was feeding these alarming reports to Washington at a time when, in Sharon own words, "strategic coordination between Israel and the U.S. has reached unprecedented dimensions." Then the invasion happened. No WMD were found. The Senate Intelligence Committee and the Israeli Knesset both released separate reports afterward. Both revealed that much of the intelligence Israel gave to the Bush administration was false. As one retired Israeli general put it: "Israeli intelligence was a full partner to the picture presented by American and British intelligence regarding Iraq's non-conventional capabilities." So the same country pushing for the war was also the source of the false intelligence used to sell the war. That is not two separate stories. That is one story. My analysis is this is the part that should end the debate. People say Bush lied. Maybe he did. But who fed him the lies? The Senate and the Knesset both did reports. Both found the same thing. Israeli intelligence was false and it was a full partner in the case for war. Then after the war turned into a disaster, Israel said it never pushed for the war. The Knesset report says otherwise. So does Sharon own spokesman. So does Peres on CNN. So does the retired general. They cannot have it both ways. They supplied the lies and then they walked away from the result. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Israel was the only country outside the United States, apart from Kuwait, where a majority of politicians and the public enthusiastically favored the Iraq war. A poll taken in early 2002 found that 58 percent of Israeli Jews believed that "Israel should encourage the United States to attack Iraq." Another poll taken a year later, in February 2003, found that 77.5 percent of Israeli Jews wanted the United States to invade Iraq. Compare that to Britain, America closest ally. A poll taken just before the war found that 51 percent of Britons opposed it, while only 39 percent supported it. In Britain 50,000 people demonstrated against the war. In Israel nobody did. Gideon Levy of Ha'aretz asked why. "Why is it that in Israel there is no public debate about whether the war is necessary?" His answer: "Israel is the only country in the West whose leaders support the war unreservedly and where no alternative opinion is voiced." Ha'aretz ran a story in February 2003 titled "Enthusiastic IDF Awaits War in Iraq." It said Israel "military and political leadership yearns for war in Iraq." The Forward ran a piece titled "Jerusalem Frets as U.S. Battles Iraq War Delays." Israel leaders wanted the war sooner, not later. Bill Clinton said in 2006 that "every Israeli politician I knew" believed Saddam was such a threat that he should be removed even if he did not have WMD. But here is the part that matters. Israel did not want Americans to know this. In fall 2002 a group of American political consultants called the Israel Project circulated a six-page memo to key Israelis and pro-Israel leaders in the US. It was titled "Talking about Iraq." It told them: "If your goal is regime change, you must be much more careful with your language because of the potential backlash. You do not want Americans to believe that the war on Iraq is being waged to protect Israel rather than to protect America." IDPs returning to Serekaniye and Afrin are facing violent attacks from mobs organized under banners of "arab tribes". The houses where they return are often looted and destroyed, facing very difficult conditions on arrival. Many of this attacks can be traced to armed groups connected to the SNA, the turkish backed militias that in theory merged into the Syrian army. At the end of October Kurdish refugees returning to Gire Spi faced heavy violence, with attackers beating kurdish IDPs and burning their cars on arrival. # INCREASING TENSIONS IN HASAKAH The neighborhood of Ghuwayran, that hosts the prisons of ISIS fighters and a majority of Arab population, has been a friction point for tensions between Kurdish and Arab populations. Demonstrations to demand that education is held in Kurdish language faced counter-demonstration from Arab population, with threatening actions against Kurdish people often being overlooked if not directly encourage by government forces. # SYRIA FLOODS On October heavy rains in Syria led to floods in Aleppo, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, Hasakah, Hama, Homs and Latakia governorates. At least 5 people lost their live due to the floods and The Syrian Civil Defense has carried out more than 300 emergency responses. Homes and refugee camps in Raqqa and Deir Ezzor had to be evacuated. Roads and bridges suffered damages from the floods, as well as power lines and other logistical infrastructure like fiber-optic cable. These floods deepened the humanitarian crisis in Syria, that together with increasing living costs are deepening the hardships that many families across Syria are suffering. # ISREAL ADVANCES IN SOUTHERN SYRIA Israel has been intensifying their operation is Southern Syria, establishing checkpoints and arresting farmers in the Quneitra region. After KDP (Kurdish Democratic Party) forced the creation of a unilateral government, PUK (Patriotic Union of Kurdistan) withdraw from the parliament and seek negotiations with Baghdad aiming to access the budget of the regions in their control separated from the rest of KRG. The already tense political situation of Iraq, impacted also by the Iran war and with ongoing debates on other Kurdish disputed areas like Sinjar and Kirkuk, is also affected by the US movements withdrawing it's military forces from the region. Negotiations to solve the current crisis are ongoing, with several Kurdish parties working to mitigate tensions and find some consensus agreements. # CLASHES IN ROJHILAT As tensions between US and Iran continue increasing, with looming threats of intensified return of hostilities beyond what took place until now, clashes between IRGC forces and YRK guerrillas of the Kurdish Liberation Movement are intensifying.
